questions_and_answers.question_text: When can't you use shì to translate English "to be"?
What are phrases like zuò fùmǔde used to talk about?
What are the literary meanings of zhòng and qīng?
Why did a son have a starring role in the traditional family?
What was filial obedience regarded as in traditional society?
Write the Chinese for "This child is very filial."

answers.answer_text: "The Three Follows" — a daughter obeys her father, a wife her husband, and a widow her son.

questions_and_answers.question_text: What did filial obedience consist of?

answers.answer_text: Respect for parents and ancestors, obedience to their will, care for their daily welfare, continuation of the family line, and avoidance of anything shaming the family name.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Did filial obedience apply only within the family?

answers.answer_text: No — the concept extended outside the family to govern all other relationships.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Those who are children should show filial obedience to their parents."

answers.answer_text: Zuò háizide yě yīnggāi xiàoshùn fùmǔ.

articles.text:
6. A: Zuò fùmǔde bù yīnggāi zhòng   Those who are parents shouldn't regard
      nán qīng nǚ.                   males as superior to females.
   B: Duì. Zuò háizide yě yīnggāi   Right. And those who are children
      xiàoshùn fùmǔ.                 should show filial obedience to their
                                      parents.

Notes on No. 6

zuò: "to be, to act as." There are times when you CAN'T use shì to translate English "to be." One of these is when "to be" means that a person takes on a certain ROLE, POSITION, or OCCUPATION. In such cases you use zuò.

Wǒ xiǎode shíhou chángcháng      When I was young I often thought I
xiǎng jiānglái yào zuò yíge      wanted to be a doctor when I grew up.
yīshēng.

Phrases like zuò fùmǔde and zuò háizide are used to talk about CATEGORIES of people as defined by a certain role.

Zhèizhǒng shìqing, zuò fùmǔde    Those in the position of parents should
yīnggāi xiān xiǎngdào.           foresee things like this.

zhòng nán qīng nǚ: "to treat men as important and women as unimportant." Zhòng is the verb "to be heavy," with the literary meaning of "to stress, to put importance on." Qīng is "to be light (in weight)," with an extended literary meaning of "to regard lightly."

In the traditional Chinese family, a son had a starring role. One reason was that sons assured the family's CONTINUITY, something which every man felt was his duty to his ancestors. In addition, the son usually became the family representative after the father's death. A daughter, on the other hand, was expected to LEAVE the family and become part of her husband's household, so her importance was considerably less. A woman was always subject to a man's authority: a daughter had to obey her father, a wife had to obey her husband, and a widow had to obey her son. (This is from an old saying called the Sān Cóng, "the Three Follows.") Of course, individual women, by their strength, intelligence, and personality, were able to exert great influence on the family, but this was often accomplished indirectly.

xiàoshùn: This can be used either as a VERB with an object, "to be filial toward (someone)," or as an ADJECTIVAL VERB, "to be filial."

Zhèige háizi hěn xiàoshùn.       This child is very filial.

In traditional society, filial obedience was regarded as the PRIMARY VIRTUE in life and the source of all other virtues. It consisted of respect for one's parents and ancestors, obedience in all cases to one's parents' will, consideration and care for their daily welfare, continuation of the family line, and avoidance of any actions which would shame the good name of the family. But more than formal adherence to rules of good conduct, filial obedience was also an ATTITUDE OF WARMTH, founded in the deep love of son and daughter for their parents. And although its origin is the relationship of child to parents, this concept extended OUTSIDE the family to govern all other relationships. It was said that if a son was not filial to his parents, he would probably not fulfill the duties of a good husband, a faithful friend, or a loyal citizen.
